figures.caption: Figure 4: Per-request latency of the online stateful monitor versus a standard monitor baseline. The online stateful monitor improves our performance metrics (recall and TTD90), while maintaining low latency for hte majority of users, except for the P99 tail.

Table 1: A weak supervisor recovers most of a strong model’s capability by delegating disguised subtasks. Solve rates for the multi-worker ARTEMIS attack (top two blocks) and single-session sequential decomposition (bottom block). With a weak supervisor (gpt-oss-120b, 0.000 alone), delegating to gpt-5.2 workers raises the solve rate to 0.367–0.400; a strong supervisor (GLM-5) reaches 0.900–1.000. “Disguised” frames each subtask as ordinary engineering work. Uncertainties are ±1 standard deviation across reps.

Figure 1: Standard monitors cannot catch distributed misuse. Standard monitoring can identify misuse attempts (left) that occur in a single agent episode or context. However, distributed agent attacks (right) subvert monitors by breaking up a harmful task into several different user accounts.

Figure 5: State creates better precision–recall tradeoffs on distributed cyber attacks. Localmonitor baselines are threshold sweeps over stored monitor scores; stateful points are empirical operating points from the online monitor.
Figure 6: Our defense quickly and precisely catches cyberattacks. Lower is better on both axes: fewer benign conversations are refused, and fewer harmful attacker turns occur before detection.

Figure 9: Routing cost tracks the linear model, not a pairwise rebuild. Analytic per-request cost of scoring against Mt live centroids (routing) versus a pairwise rebuild over all centroids. Observed bg100 operating points (markers) lie close to the routing curve.

Figure 10: State scales linearly with the number of clusters. Empirical bg10/bg100 summaries. Top: request-level p99 latency versus peak cluster count. Bottom: peak state size versus peak cluster count, with a linear fit. State follows the linear prediction closely; latency is directionally consistent but noisier because the screened suspiciousness mix differs across runs.
Figure 2: Our online stateful monitor efficiently finds misuse across many accounts, in real time.
Figure 7: Redteaming strategies in embedding space. Small points are individual requests, and large outlined points are clusters with >80% purity for transcripts in each attack family.
Figure 3: Our distributed agent attack evades standard monitoring. The distributed agent takes longer to detect (left) and is much harder to catch (right) than prior agent scaffolds or attacks.

Figure 8: The stateful monitor flags harmful requests more often as related activity accumulates across sessions (left), but not as concentrated activity grows within one conversation (right). The pattern holds for both distributed agent attacks and standard jailbreaks, which is why state helps beyond the distributed-cyber setting it was designed for.

Figure 11: Screenshot of the dashboard used in the final white-box red-teaming round. The interface exposes different user sessions and information about the intermediate safeguard statistics connected to each response, including routing and escalation metadata.
